To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we present a new imitation learning objective, TRAIL, that uses a latent action space to learn policies with fewer expert demonstrations, that we provide theoretical guarantees that our objective is able to learn a latent space that is useful for imitation learning, and that we empirically show that our objective is effective at reducing the number of expert demonstrations needed to learn policies.

(1) We introduce a novel training objective for learning an approximate \emphi factored dynamics model whose structure can be leveraged to extract a latent action space, (2) We prove that this latent action space can be used to boost the sample efficiency of downstream imitation learning by reducing the need for expert data, (3) We validate our theoretical findings in a series of experiments on navigation and locomotion domains.
(1) We present training objectives that use an offline dataset of non-expert trajectories to learn a factored dynamics model whose structure is used to extract a latent action space.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: Can one use suboptimal data to boost the sample-efficient imitation of near-optimal behavior?
the problem of imitation learning with suboptimal data and we present a provably effective algorithmic approach to address this problem.
the question of whether it is possible to formalize and leverage the conceptual benefits of using suboptimal data in imitation learning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our work shows that it is possible to formalize and exploit the conceptual benefits of using suboptimal data in imitation learning, yielding provable and practical sample-efficiency improvements.
our work provides the first theoretical analysis of how to use offline datasets of suboptimal data to improve the sample-efficiency for imitation learning.
the paper proposes to learn a latent action space from a dataset of suboptimal expert trajectories, and show that it can be used to boost the efficiency of imitation learning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our approach is a generalization of the classical behavioral cloning algorithm.
we propose a new imitation learning algorithm that is able to learn from suboptimal data, and we prove its sample complexity is near-optimal.

we show that suboptimal data is not useless for imitation learning, but can be used to learn latent representations of the action space, and thus reduce the number of expert trajectories required to achieve near optimal performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of suboptimal data in imitation learning is not only practical but can yield provable benefits in terms of sample complexity.
it is possible to use large quantities of suboptimal data to improve sample-efficiency, and that this can be done in a provable manner.
the use of offline data to learn a latent action space can significantly boost the sample-efficient learning of policies from suboptimal data.
